title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: How Yo-Yos Work
summary: Rerun of an older Stuff You Should Know episode, presented as part of the "12 Days of Christmas Toys" playlist, about how yo-yos work. The hosts trace yo-yo etymology (yo meaning "come" in Filipino, earlier hunting and roll-call uses, and the post-WWII Italian-Philadelphia slang), the history from ancient toys through the Filipino design and Pedro Flores, Donald Duncan's purchase and the "yo-yo" trademark loss in 1965, the Duncan company's bankruptcy and move to Luck, Wisconsin, and the physics of sleeping and walking the dog: linear and angular momentum, gyroscopic stability, moment of inertia, and the ball-bearing and clutch ("yo-yo with a brain") modifications. Trivia includes Abbie Hoffman's 1968 HUAC appearance, Nixon being given a yo-yo at the Grand Ole Opry, and the NASA Toys in Space yo-yo test in microgravity. The episode closes with a listener mail about a charity album for Japan earthquake relief.

segments.title: Rerun intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as part of the 12 Days of Christmas Toys playlist. The hosts banter about back scratching and promise a physics-heavy yo-yo episode.

segments.title: Etymology of 'yo'
segments.summary: Chuck discusses the Eddie Murphy film Harlem Nights and its anachronistic use of 'yo'. He says 'yo' was used as a hunting cry as early as the 15th century, as a sailor call and roll-call response by 1859, and that the modern slang came from Italian quarters of Philadelphia after World War Two.

segments.title: Ancient and early yo-yo forms
segments.summary: The hosts discuss early yo-yos, including a claim of ancient Greek or Chinese origin more than 2,500 years ago, and the older design with the string tied tightly to the axle, popular in Europe under names such as the bandolore and the lirigoo-type toys.

segments.title: Napoleon and European yo-yo popularity
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the yo-yo's popularity in Europe, a painting of a French Louis holding one, the hoop-on-a-stick toy, and a claim that Napoleon used a yo-yo for stress relief.

segments.title: Filipino design and early hunting weapon
segments.summary: The modern loose-string Filipino design lets the yo-yo spin at the end of the string. The hosts describe the early Philippine version as a large hunting weapon with a rope and spikes, later made smaller into toys.

segments.title: Pedro Flores, Donald Duncan and the trademark
segments.summary: Pedro Flores started the first modern yo-yo company in the US in the 1920s and sold to Donald Duncan in 1929. Duncan trademarked the name, but federal courts ruled in 1965 that yo-yo was generic.

segments.title: Duncan company bankruptcy and Luck, Wisconsin
segments.summary: Legal fights drained the Duncan company, which went bankrupt. It moved to Luck, Wisconsin, in the 1940s, made maple yo-yos at high volume, and reportedly sold 45 million in 1962. National Yo-Yo Day is June 6, Donald Duncan's birthday. The Duncan name was later sold and lives on.

segments.title: Teaser before physics
segments.summary: Chuck briefly teases an extra piece of history before moving on to the physics segment.

segments.title: Momentum and gyroscopic stability
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the classic loose-string yo-yo has linear momentum up and down and angular momentum from spinning on the axle. Angular momentum increases as it falls, allowing it to sleep. Gyroscopic stability keeps a spinning yo-yo from changing its axis, compared to a football or a knuckleball.

segments.title: Waking the yo-yo and tricks
segments.summary: A tug on the string increases friction in the loop and rewinds the yo-yo. Sleeping is key to tricks such as walking the dog, cat's cradle, and around the world.

segments.title: Moment of inertia and vintage design
segments.summary: The hosts explain that moment of inertia rises when mass sits further from the axis, so yo-yos with weight on the outside sleep longer. They discuss the inverted vintage Duncan designs and the 1960s improvements of adding outer mass and extending the axle.

segments.title: Design modifications and the ball bearing yo-yo
segments.summary: The hosts call later changes modifications rather than improvements. The ball bearing design splits the axle into inner and outer races so the string stops affecting spin, letting the yo-yo sleep much longer.

segments.title: Yo-yo with a brain (clutch yo-yo) and modifications
segments.summary: The 1990s Yomega yo-yo with a brain uses weighted clutch arms and springs that release the spindle at speed, so it spins for a time then reengages and returns. Michael Caffrey invented it, and Tom Cune's No Jive yo-yo, which could be taken apart, came out two years earlier.

segments.title: Physics recap and terminology
segments.summary: Chuck summarizes the physics. Josh says teachers use yo-yos to explain physics properties, and the hosts sort out which term is angular momentum and which is gyroscopic stability or moment of inertia.

segments.title: Yo-yo trivia: Abbie Hoffman, Nixon and NASA
segments.summary: In 1968 Abbie Hoffman walked the dog during a House Un-American Activities Committee session and was charged with contempt of Congress. In 1974 Nixon was given a yo-yo at the Grand Ole Opry and struggled with it. NASA's Toys in Space project tested a yo-yo in microgravity in 1985, where it spun but did not sleep.

segments.title: Search tip and yo-yo Ma aside
segments.summary: The hosts discuss searching for yo-yo results without unrelated hits such as Yo-Yo Ma, Gabba Gabba, and MTV, using a minus sign before terms. The rapper Neo is mentioned.

segments.title: Pointer to the HowStuffWorks article
segments.summary: Chuck recommends the yo-yo article on the HowStuffWorks site, which has illustrations, and introduces listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: charity album for Japan
segments.summary: A listener from the band New Century Classics asks for a shout-out to a charity compilation album of 37 tracks by 37 artists that raises funds for relief after the Japanese earthquake and nuclear disaster, available at MoreHopeForJapan.com.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and invite listeners to send feedback via social media or email, and point to HowStuffWorks for more.
